notes.b: Every sport has written rules, but not every situation is covered by them. Ethics and fair play describe how people are expected to behave in those gaps and within the rules.
points: Ethics in sport means the moral principles about what is right and wrong that guide behaviour in sport, so they shape what players, coaches and officials choose to do, not just what the rulebook says.
Fair play means playing within the rules and the spirit of the game (the idea behind the rules, not only their wording), with respect for others.

Ethical practice in sport rests on four principles: integrity, respect, fairness and equity. Each one is taught in the blocks that follow, with its definition, examples, breaches (ways of breaking it) and why it matters.
notes.tip: You may be asked to identify three principles of ethical practice, or to list two and outline why upholding them matters. Learn all four names: integrity, respect, fairness and equity.

notes.b: Integrity is the principle about honesty. It is tested most when breaking the rules would go unnoticed, so it is about what a person does when nobody would find out.
points: Definition: honesty and strong moral principles, shown by doing the right thing when no one is watching.
In practice: owning up to touching the ball last, even when the referee has not seen it, because the honest call is made even though it costs the player something.
In practice: not diving or feigning injury (pretending to be fouled or hurt) to win a free or a penalty.
In practice: refusing to dope (use banned performance-enhancing substances), even when no one is watching.
Breach: doping, or match-fixing, where the outcome of a contest is arranged in advance for gain.
Why it matters: integrity lets players, officials and spectators trust the sport and its results, because they know the outcome was not secretly manipulated.
Applied to Gaelic football: a player who tells the referee about a foul the referee missed shows integrity, even though it costs the player's team a free.
notes.tip: If asked to define integrity and outline its importance to an activity, give the definition (honesty and strong moral principles, doing the right thing when no one is watching), then say it builds trust in results and in the sport. Be ready to name a second principle as well.

notes.b: Respect is about how you treat everyone and everything involved in a game, not only the people on the opposing team. It is what keeps a game safe and pleasant to be part of.
points: Definition: regard for opponents, team-mates, officials, coaches, spectators, the rules and oneself.
In practice: accepting officials' decisions, even when a player disagrees with them, because the official's role is to apply the rules and the game cannot work if every call is argued.
In practice: shaking hands with opponents and officials at the end of a match, which shows regard for them whatever the result.
Breach: abuse of officials, sledging (insulting or taunting an opponent to unsettle them), or violence towards an opponent.
Why it matters: a safe, positive environment keeps players and officials involved, so clubs can retain them (stop them leaving the sport).
Applied to hurling: a player who stays calm after a hard tackle, rather than retaliating (hitting back), shows respect for the opponent and the rules.
notes.tip: Respect covers more than opponents: remember officials, coaches, spectators, the rules and oneself too. Its importance is a safe, positive environment and keeping players and officials.

notes.b: Fairness is about a level playing field. If everyone is treated and judged the same way, the result means something.
points: Definition: everyone competes under the same rules and conditions, and no one seeks an unfair advantage.
In practice: consistent refereeing, applying the same rules to both teams, so neither side is helped or hindered by the official.
In practice: fair team selection, based on ability and commitment rather than favouritism.
Breach: cheating, which gives one competitor an advantage the rules do not allow.
Breach: win-at-all-costs coaching, where winning is put above the rules and above the players' welfare (their health and wellbeing).
Why it matters: the result reflects ability and effort rather than an unfair advantage.
Applied to athletics: every runner in a race starts under the same start rules and runs the same distance, so the placings reflect running ability.
notes.tip: When explaining the importance of fairness, link it to the result: it should reflect ability and effort. Be ready to give consistent refereeing, fair team selection and no cheating as examples.

notes.b: Equity is easily confused with equality, but the two differ. Equity recognises that people start from different positions, so some need different support to get the same chance.
points: Definition: giving everyone access and opportunity according to their needs, so that differences in gender, ability, disability, ethnicity or income do not exclude people.
Equity differs from equality: equality treats everyone the same, while equity gives people what they need for a fair chance.
In practice: equal facilities and coaching for girls' teams as for boys' teams, so gender does not limit the standard of training a team receives.
Breach: discrimination (unfair treatment of a person because of who they are), such as excluding a player because of gender, disability, ethnicity or income.
Why it matters: removing barriers lets people from every group take part and compete.
Applied to Gaelic football: a club that gives a player with a disability adapted equipment (equipment changed to suit the player's needs) and coaching gives that player the same chance to take part.
notes.tip: Define the difference between equity and equality once, clearly: equality treats everyone the same, equity gives people what they need. If asked to explain the importance of equity in a named activity, use that activity in your answer.

notes.h: Who is responsible for ethical practice
notes.b: Ethical practice does not rest with players alone. Everyone connected with a sport has a part to play, and each group's role is different.
points: Participants: responsible for their own conduct towards opponents, team-mates and officials.
Coaches and leaders: model good behaviour (set an example by how they act themselves) and teach fair play.
Officials: apply the rules impartially (without favouring either side) to every competitor.
Parents and spectators: responsible for their behaviour on the sideline and in the stands.
National governing bodies (NGBs) and sports bodies: write codes (written standards of behaviour), provide education, and impose sanctions (punishments) on those who breach the principles.

notes.b: Upholding the four principles is not just about being nice. It affects the people playing, the people watching and the future of the sport itself.
points: Safety and welfare: ethical conduct protects participants from injury and abuse.
Enjoyment and participation: a sport with fair play keeps people playing and attracts new players.
Credibility of results: results carry weight (are believed and respected) only when every competitor has followed the rules.
Sponsorship and image: sponsors (businesses that pay to be linked with a sport) and the public judge a sport by its conduct, so ethical behaviour protects its image and sponsorship.
Values for life: fair play teaches honesty, respect and fairness that carry over beyond sport.
notes.tip: A case study may ask you to explain how a doping athlete did not adhere to at least two principles of ethical practice. Use generic reasoning: doping breaks integrity (not honest) and fairness (an unfair advantage). Doping has its own subsections, so keep it to the principles here.

keyTerms.definition: The moral principles about what is right and wrong that guide behaviour in sport.
Playing within the rules and the spirit of the game, with respect for others.
Honesty and strong moral principles, shown by doing the right thing when no one is watching.
Regard for opponents, team-mates, officials, coaches, spectators, the rules and oneself.
Competing under the same rules and conditions, without seeking an unfair advantage.
Giving everyone access and opportunity according to their needs, so that they have a fair chance.
Treating everyone the same, whatever their needs.
Excluding or treating people unfairly because of characteristics such as gender, disability, ethnicity or income.
Arranging the outcome of a contest, or part of it, in advance for gain.
Coaching that puts winning above the rules and the other principles of ethical practice.
The body that governs a sport at national level.

questions.prompt: Explain two principles of ethical practice and outline the importance of upholding them in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Activity: Gaelic football. Integrity means honesty and doing the right thing when no one is watching. A player who tells the referee about a foul the referee missed, rather than staying silent, shows integrity, and this matters because it lets players, officials and spectators trust the result. Fairness means everyone competes under the same rules and no one seeks an unfair advantage. A referee who applies the same rules to both teams, and a team that selects players on ability and commitment, show fairness. Upholding fairness means the result reflects the ability and effort of the teams, so the sport stays credible and players keep taking part. Upholding both principles also protects players' safety and the sport's image, which helps clubs keep attracting members.

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of equity in a named physical activity.
questions.model: Activity: athletics. Equity gives everyone access and opportunity according to their needs, so that differences in gender, ability, disability, ethnicity or income do not exclude people. In athletics, equity means athletes with a disability receive adapted equipment and coaching, and girls' clubs receive the same facilities and coaching as boys' clubs, so every athlete has a fair chance to compete. Without equity, talented athletes are excluded for reasons unrelated to ability, so the sport loses potential competitors and its pool of talent shrinks.

Respect: a player who accepts the referee's decision without dissent and shakes hands with the opposing players at the end of the match. 3. Fairness: a referee who applies the same rules to both teams, so that the result depends on ability and effort.
